stem: An adult patient receives a lawful 14-day outpatient prescription for buprenorphine-naloxone specifically for treatment of opioid use disorder. A staff member says Massachusetts' seven-day initial-opiate statute automatically requires the prescription to be reduced to seven days. What is the best response to that specific claim?

choices.text: Agree, because every medication related to an opioid is subject to the seven-day statute regardless of indication.

Disagree. The seven-day statute expressly does not apply to medications designed for treatment of substance abuse or opioid dependence; the prescription must instead satisfy the other laws governing its OUD pathway.
Agree unless the patient has previously filled an opioid prescription in Massachusetts.
Disagree because buprenorphine-naloxone becomes Massachusetts Schedule VI when used for OUD.
Reduce the quantity to seven days without prescriber involvement because pharmacists may unilaterally rewrite any opioid prescription to comply with supply limits.

explanation.core_reasoning: M.G.L. c. 94C, § 19D(c) excludes medications designed for treatment of substance abuse or opioid dependence from the seven-day supply statute. That exclusion answers the narrow seven-day question; it does not waive the separate federal and state requirements that govern buprenorphine-naloxone and OUD treatment.

choice_analysis.A: Incorrect. Section 19D contains an express treatment-indication exclusion.
choice_analysis.B: Correct. The seven-day statute itself does not apply to the described OUD-treatment medication, while other applicable prescribing/dispensing rules remain in force.
choice_analysis.C: Incorrect. The statutory exclusion here turns on the OUD-treatment purpose, not prior opioid-fill history.
choice_analysis.D: Incorrect. Buprenorphine-naloxone remains Schedule III; the result comes from the § 19D treatment exclusion.
choice_analysis.E: Incorrect. The statutory issue does not create a general pharmacist power to rewrite a prescription.

related_facts: The adult first-outpatient seven-day rule and the OUD-treatment exclusion must be read together.
explanation.mpje_trap: Do not stop at the word 'opioid'; first determine whether the statute expressly excludes the treatment pathway.

reasoning_steps: Identify the medication and its stated OUD-treatment purpose
Apply the express § 19D(c) exclusion before applying the seven-day ceiling
Keep separate OUD prescribing/dispensing requirements outside the narrow question
